newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian race row MP softens stand.
newsitem.headline: Australian race row MP softens stand.

text.p: Australian race row politician Pauline Hanson has softened her divisive stand against Asian immigration and welfare for Aborigines, saying Asians had a place in Australia, newspapers reported on Saturday.

"Asians have always had a presence in Australia and always will have," Hanson was quoted as saying. Her views on race and welfare have struck a chord with some voters but sparked violent protests from others,.
The national daily, The Australian, quoted Hanson as telling a radio station in the provincial city of Newcastle that she only opposed high immigration because of the environmental damage.

She had previously warned Australia was in danger of being swamped by Asians, who have "their own culture and religion and form ghettos and do not assimilate", and warned half the population would be Asian by 2040.

Hanson, who once said she was fighting for "anyone apart from Aborigines and Torres Strait islanders" and has criticised Aboriginal welfare, also said she was concerned about living standards for native Australians, papers said. About 2,500 protesters jeered and jostled Hanson supporters as they arrived to hear her address a rally promoting her new One Nation Party in Newcastle on Friday.
Security was heavy, with hundreds of police present and surrounding streets closed off.

Hanson was smuggled into the building by police hours before her scheduled appearance. Sydney's Daily Telegraph newspaper said a police helicopter was on standby to help her escape if the protest turned violent.

The mother of four from conservative Queensland state was elected to the national parliament as an independent after being dumped by Prime Minister John Howard's Liberal party during the 1996 election campaign over comments criticised as racist.
Her recently formed One Nation Party has been steadily wooing voters and her rallies around the country have drawn thousands of supporters, as well as thousands of protesters.
Leading opinion polls now rank One Nation as the third most popular political group after the ruling Liberal-National coalition and the Labor opposition.
One Nation's poll support, above 10 percent in all major polls and growing, ranks it well ahead of the traditional third force in Australian politics, the Australian Democrats
